opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that in robot RL you usually have two kinds of reward terms. There are the ones that actually describe the task, like "track this velocity command" or "get to that point," and the ones that describe how you want the behavior to look: penalize joint torques, penalize jerky actions, keep the feet from slipping. Then there's a third category that people often add, which is basically there to help the agent explore. Little shaping terms that nudge it in the right direction early in training so it doesn't get stuck.

The problem with that third category is that it doesn't describe what you want at the end. It's a crutch for the optimization. Once the policy has learned the task, those terms are still in the reward, and now they're pulling the final behavior somewhere you didn't intend. So you end up in a loop of tuning weights, getting one thing working, and realizing it broke something else. It's very brittle, and it doesn't transfer. If you change the robot or the terrain, all that careful balancing has to be redone.

So what I've tried to do instead is keep the reward as close as possible to a clean description of the task plus the behavior constraints, and solve exploration some other way. One big tool for that is a curriculum. On rough terrain, for example, you start the robot on easy, flat ground and only move it to harder terrain once it's succeeding. The environment does the guiding, not the reward. Massive parallel simulation helps a lot too. When you have thousands of robots training at once, you get far more diverse experience, and many exploration problems become much less severe. You can also do things on the environment side, like how you initialize the robots or how you sample commands, so the agent naturally sees the situations it needs to learn from.

The nice outcome is that the reward stays interpretable. When something goes wrong, you can look at it and reason about why, instead of wondering which of fifteen shaping terms is fighting which. And it makes the whole pipeline much more reusable across tasks and robots, which in the end is what you want if RL is going to be a practical engineering tool rather than an art.

r001.rationale: The response says exploration shaping is brittle and does not transfer: changing the robot or terrain requires redoing the weight balancing, and the pipeline should be reusable across tasks and robots.

r002.rationale: The response proposes curricula, parallel simulation, and environment-side choices to support exploration. It does not mention human demonstrations as a substitute.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the honest answer is that it almost never works the way you want it to, and when it does work it tends to be very fragile. Every time you add a reward term just to get the robot to explore, like a bonus for visiting new states or a penalty for standing still, you're introducing something that has nothing to do with the task you actually care about. And the policy will happily optimize that term instead of the real objective. You end up spending days tuning the weight so that it's big enough to kick the robot out of the local minimum but small enough that it doesn't dominate at the end, and the moment you change the task slightly, or the robot morphology, or the simulation parameters, all of that tuning goes out the window.

What we found with legged locomotion is that the exploration problem is usually a symptom of something else. The robot is stuck because the task is too hard at the start, or because the terrain is too difficult, or because the reward landscape has a big flat region early on. So rather than patching that with intrinsic rewards, we'd rather fix the problem at the source. Curriculum is the big one for us. If you start the robot on flat ground and only move it to stairs and gaps once it's actually walking, you don't need any exploration bonus at all, the gradient is just there from the beginning. Same thing with how we design the environments, how we terminate episodes, how we initialize states. Those are all much more direct levers than a reward term.

And the other piece is scale. When you're simulating thousands of robots in parallel, you're getting an enormous amount of data per second, and a lot of the exploration happens almost for free just because of the diversity across environments and the stochasticity of the policy. So a lot of the tricks that made sense when you had a single agent collecting data slowly just aren't necessary anymore.

The last thing I'd say is that it's also about trusting what you end up with. If the final behavior comes out of a clean task reward plus some physically motivated regularization, I know why the robot is doing what it does. If it came out of a cocktail of exploration bonuses, I'm much less sure what it actually learned, and that matters a lot when you're going to deploy it on real hardware.

r001.rationale: The response says exploration-reward tuning must be redone when the task or robot changes, so it does not transfer across robot tasks.

r002.rationale: The response recommends curriculum and environment design, but does not propose human demonstrations as a substitute for tuned exploration rewards.

astra-6.text:
Because then you’re mixing two different things: specifying what you want the robot to do and helping the algorithm discover how to do it. Ideally, the reward should describe the task. If you keep adding terms just to encourage exploration, you can end up changing the behavior you’re actually optimizing for.

It also becomes a lot of manual work. A reward that helps learning in one setup might need to be tuned again when you change the robot or the task. So we try to handle exploration through the learning setup as much as possible and keep the reward focused on the behavior we want.

r001.rationale: The response says exploration rewards require more manual tuning when the robot or task changes, communicating that this approach does not scale across tasks.

sol-6.1.text:
Because then you’re solving two problems with the same reward: specifying what you want the robot to do and helping it discover how to do it. If it doesn’t learn, it becomes hard to tell whether the objective is wrong or whether it simply hasn’t explored the right behavior yet.

You can add rewards for intermediate behaviors to guide it, but that introduces assumptions about how the task should be solved. The policy may exploit those rewards or learn something that looks good according to the reward but isn’t what you actually wanted. And then you spend a lot of time tuning weights.

So I prefer to keep the reward focused on the task and address exploration separately as much as possible. That makes it easier to understand what’s working and to reuse the approach across tasks.

r001.rationale: The response says intermediate rewards require assumptions and weight tuning, and prefers an approach that is easier to reuse across tasks. It does not clearly state that manually shaping exploration rewards does not scale across robot tasks.

r002.rationale: The response does not propose human demonstrations as a substitute for manually tuned exploration rewards.
